title: Wi-Fi forensics basics
quick: Wi-Fi forensics studies wireless traffic and device records, such as captured 802.11 frames, access point logs and saved network lists, to show which devices were present or connected.

sections.title: Two kinds of evidence
text: Wi-Fi evidence comes from the air and from devices. Over the air, a capture adapter in monitor mode can record frames from the wireless network. On devices, operating systems keep lists of known networks and connection history.
Access points and controllers also keep logs of which device connected and when.

sections.title: Monitor mode and channels
text: In monitor mode, an adapter records all frames on the selected channel, from every network, not only your own. It can capture only one channel at a time. Hopping across channels helps find networks but loses packets, so a fixed channel is better when you study one access point. Not every adapter or driver supports this.
Management and control frames are normally hidden by drivers and are visible only in monitor mode.

sections.title: What can be learned
text: Frames show device hardware addresses (MAC addresses), network names (SSIDs) and when devices joined or left. They can show that a device was near an access point. Content of protected networks cannot be read by a passive capture without the right keys.
points: MAC address: can be randomised by modern phones, so it may not identify a device over time.
SSID: the name of a network, which can be copied by anyone.
Access point logs: often the most useful source for who connected.

sections.title: Care and limits
text: Capturing other people's wireless traffic may be restricted. Procedures and laws differ by country and agency, so follow your lab's own procedure.
Signal location is only approximate. Do not claim an exact place from signal alone.

mistakes: Treating a MAC address as a fixed identity when it may be randomised.
Forgetting that an adapter in monitor mode sees only one channel.
Trusting an SSID, which an attacker can copy.

terms.meaning: The name of a wireless network.
A hardware address used by a network interface.
An adapter mode that records all frames on a channel.
A device that connects wireless clients to a network.
A frame used to join, leave and manage a wireless network.

exam.a: It lets the adapter record all frames on a channel, including management frames, from networks other than your own.

exam.q: Why is a MAC address not always reliable?
exam.a: Many devices use random addresses for privacy, so one device can appear under several addresses.
